_about: Every change to a scheduling policy must have an entry here before it can be
merged. Each entry states the mechanism (why it should help, in terms of the
algorithm), the measurement that decides it, and the decision with its reason.
Numbers are NOT written here. The generator reads them out of the artifact
named in `measurement.artifact` and renders them into OPTIMIZATIONS.md, so the
prose cannot drift from the data. What is written here is the claim: the
direction the change is expected to move the result. scripts/render_optimizations.py
checks that claim against the artifact and fails if the two disagree.
accepted     measured better, and the mechanism explains why
rejected     measured worse or dominated; kept in the doc so it is not retried
inconclusive measured effect too small to separate from noise, or untested in
proposed     mechanism argued, not yet measured. Cannot merge in this state.

baseline.note: The published ECTD implementation. Every delta below is against this unless stated.

reference.note: The strongest published baseline on this corpus. Reported alongside so a change is not called a win for beating ECTD alone.

entries.title: Weight the task's own execution cost twice in the processor score
mechanism: `_place_scored` scores a candidate processor as `eft + tail`, where `eft` is
`start + w[task][q]` and the tail is the optimistic cost of everything AFTER
the task. So the score is `start + 1*w + continuation`.
This variant scores `eft + (w + continuation)`, which is `start + 2*w +
continuation`. The task's own execution cost is counted twice.
That is not a correction of an error. Stock ECTD's estimator is already the
unbiased one: `start + w + continuation` is the actual finish time of this
task plus the estimated cost of what follows. Counting `w` twice is a
deliberate bias toward the processor where THIS task runs fastest, at the
expense of the tail estimate.
It helps because the tail estimate is the unreliable half of the score. The
optimistic cost table assumes every successor lands on its best processor and
that no contention occurs, which is systematically optimistic once several
tasks compete for the same processors. The own-cost term is concrete and
known. Weighting it up trades a noisy forecast for a certain local cost, and
on this corpus that trade pays.

claim.statement: At least 1% better than stock ECTD pooled, and not worse than AEFT.

decision: Accepted. Largest single improvement measured on this corpus, and the only
change that beats AEFT pooled. The mechanism above is the reason to believe it
generalises rather than being a corpus artifact: it is a bias toward measured
cost over estimated cost, which should pay wherever the tail estimate is
optimistic.
The value 2 is now measured as a plateau, not a lucky point. The sweep in
scripts/ectd_search.py scores self_weight from 0.0 to 3.0 on a 282-instance
stratified sample (one instance from every family x level x processor cell).
The curve is smooth and single-peaked: 0.0 is catastrophic (+57.3% vs stock),
2.0 sits at the top of a broad basin, with 1.5 and 3.0 both within 1.5 points.
That shape is what a real effect looks like; a lucky point would not have
smooth neighbours on both sides.
self_weight = 0.0 is worth keeping in mind as a sanity check on the whole
harness: it means ignore the task's own cost entirely and place purely on
start + tail, and it is 57% worse than stock. The own-cost term is doing real
work, not decoration.

outcome.statement: Measured at least 1% faster than stock ECTD pooled.

entries.title: Damp only the tail, not the task's own measured cost
mechanism: own_cost sets the score to `start + w + (w + continuation)`, counting the
task's own execution cost twice. The damping multiplier from the author code
was then dropped, because at self_weight 1.0 it is worth only 0.12% and the
first ablation measured the undamped version as marginally better.
That was the wrong conclusion from a real measurement. Damping is not
worthless; it was being applied to the wrong thing. The multiplier exists to
correct an over-optimistic tail estimate. The task's own execution cost is
measured, not estimated, so there is nothing optimistic about it to correct.
Damping the whole own-cost tail therefore damps a quantity that does not need
it, which is why its benefit appeared to vanish as self_weight rose.
This variant multiplies only the continuation by the damping weights and
leaves the own cost alone: `tail = w + continuation * weights`. The
correction now lands exactly on the part of the estimate that is optimistic.

claim.statement: At least as good as own_cost, i.e. damping the tail alone recovers the damping benefit without giving up the own-cost gain.

outcome.statement: Measured faster than own_cost on the full corpus, and the best configuration measured so far.

decision: Accepted. Best pooled result measured on this corpus: 1366.94, which is
-6.78% against stock ECTD and -1.02% against AEFT.
The size of the gain is small (0.12% over own_cost) and on its own would not
justify an entry. What justifies it is that the mechanism predicted the sign
and the reason: damping should help once it is applied only to the estimated
part. It does, and it helps at a self_weight where damping the whole tail was
measured as slightly harmful. A 0.12% move in the predicted direction, with a
mechanism that explains why the earlier measurement said otherwise, is worth
more than a 0.12% move on its own.
Honest limit: 0.12% is close to the resolution of this corpus. The ordering
against own_cost is consistent across the 282-instance stratified sweep and
the 2094-instance full run, which is why it is accepted, but it should not be
described as a large effect. It is a small correction that happens to be in
the right direction for a stated reason.
Still open: the per-family picture is unchanged. This configuration beats
AEFT on FFT, Genome, LIGO and Montage, and loses on GE (+1.54%) and LA
(+2.86%). Those two families are where the remaining gain is, and they are a
separate problem from the pooled score.

entries.title: Replace descendant ranks with mean own-cost-plus-tail priority
mechanism: ECTD orders ready tasks by `descendant_ranks`, which sums the DCT of every
distinct descendant. That grows with fan-out, so it favours tasks with many
downstream nodes. AEFT instead orders by the mean of own-cost-plus-tail.
The argument for it: descendant ranks double-count breadth, so a wide but
shallow task can outrank a task on the true critical path. A mean over the
per-processor estimate is smoother and does not reward fan-out on its own.

claim.statement: At least as good as own_cost, i.e. the ranking change is not a regression.

decision: Rejected. It is better than stock ECTD but worse than own_cost alone, so the
ranking change gives back part of the gain the scoring change produced. The
mechanism argument is plausible but the measurement does not support it on
this corpus.
Worth noting it is the best policy on FFT and GE, the two families where
own_cost is weakest. That is a real signal and the reason this is recorded as
rejected-rather-than-deleted: a per-family or per-regime ranking switch is a
legitimate thing to try, but it must be tried as its own entry with its own
mechanism, not smuggled in as a global change.

outcome.statement: Measured slower than own_cost, so the ranking change gives back part of the gain.

entries.title: Fall back to pure EFT when a task has more successors than processors
mechanism: AEFT's selection rule: once outdegree exceeds the processor count, the
optimistic tail is close to meaningless because the successors cannot all run
in parallel anyway. In that regime, ignore the tail and place on earliest
finish time alone.
The argument for it: the tail term is most wrong exactly where contention is
highest, so switching it off there should be strictly better than trusting it.

claim.statement: At least as good as own_cost.

decision: Rejected. Statistically indistinguishable from own_cost_aeft_ranks and worse
than own_cost. The regime switch does not pay on this corpus.
It does have the most shared wins of any policy (323), which means it is
often tied for best rather than beaten. It is a safe configuration, not a
winning one. Recorded so it is not proposed again without new evidence.

outcome.statement: Measured slower than own_cost, so the regime switch does not pay.

entries.title: Remove the critical-successor damping multiplier entirely
mechanism: The author code multiplies the tail by a weight below 1 when a task has more
than p+1 successors, derived from the critical successor's share of the
remaining rank. Removing it means trusting the raw optimistic tail.
The argument for it: the damping rule is an undocumented heuristic with an
arbitrary threshold and a rounding step. If the tail is already optimistic,
damping it further is hard to justify. Simpler is better if it costs nothing.

claim.statement: Removing damping is expected to be worse, i.e. the damping earns its place.

decision: Rejected as a standalone change, but the reason is narrower than first
recorded and the entry needs that correction.
At stock self_weight=1.0 the damping multiplier is worth only 0.12%. The
ablation measured +0.26% for removing it, which is the same effect seen from
the other side and is inside what this corpus resolves. So damping is a small
positive, not the load-bearing heuristic the first version of this entry
claimed.
What the sweep adds: damping's value shrinks as self_weight rises. At 1.5 it
is worth 0.20%, at 2.0 it is 0.10%, and at 3.0 it flips to -0.13%, i.e.
damping becomes mildly harmful. Per family at self_weight=2.0 it is +0.49% on
Montage, +0.05% on Genome, +0.15% on LA, and negative on GE (-0.25%) and LIGO
Conclusion: keep damping, because at the operating point it is a small win,
but do not describe it as essential. It is a marginal heuristic whose benefit
is being crowded out by the own-cost term. If self_weight is ever pushed
higher, damping should be re-tested rather than assumed.

outcome.statement: Measured slower than stock ECTD, so the damping earns its place.

entries.title: Apply damping above outdegree p instead of p+1
mechanism: The author code damps only when outdegree exceeds p+1. Lowering the threshold
to p damps one more task per processor count, on the theory that contention
starts one task earlier than the code assumes.
The argument for it: p+1 is a suspiciously specific threshold with no
derivation in the source. If the true crossover is p, this recovers a small
amount of accuracy for free.

claim.statement: Expected to be marginally better than stock ECTD.

decision: Inconclusive. The measured move is a fraction of a percent, which is inside
what this corpus can resolve. It is not evidence of an improvement and not
evidence of harm.
It must not be adopted on this basis, and it must not be adopted in
combination with own_cost either: the two were never measured together, and
damping interacts with the tail that own_cost reweights. Testing that
combination is a legitimate next step and needs its own entry.

outcome.statement: Measured within 0.10% of stock ECTD, which this corpus cannot resolve.

entries.title: Disable entry-task duplication
mechanism: ECTD places a copy of the entry task on every processor where a local copy
finishes before any remote successor could arrive. Disabling it prices that
step: if duplication is worthless, removing it should be neutral or better,
since each copy occupies a real processor interval.
The argument for it: duplication consumes real execution slots. On a
communication-light instance it should be pure waste.

claim.statement: Disabling duplication is expected to be worse, i.e. duplication earns its place.

decision: Rejected. Duplication measurably helps, so it stays. The cost of the copies is
outweighed by the communication it avoids.
Recorded because entry duplication is the step most likely to look like
superfluous complexity to a reader of the source, and this is the measurement
that says otherwise.

outcome.statement: Measured slower than stock ECTD, so duplication earns its place.

entries.title: Control: reimplementation must reproduce published ECTD exactly
mechanism: Not an optimization. This is the control that makes every other entry
meaningful: `v_baseline` reimplements stock ECTD inside the variant harness,
so if it does not reproduce the published `ECTD` figure exactly, the harness
is measuring something other than what it claims and no delta below is
trustworthy.
It is listed as an entry because it is a claim that must be checked on every
run, not a one-time assertion.

claim.statement: Pooled makespan must equal published ECTD to within rounding.

decision: Accepted as a control. It reproduces ECTD to the cent on every run so far,
which is the precondition for reading any other row in the table.

outcome.statement: Measured identical to published ECTD to within rounding.
